extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules for punctuation, hyphenation, word-division, and related typographic conventions intended to guide preparing copy for publication (usage for colons, semicolons, commas, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens, divisions, and basic footnote practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colons (rules 132–136)
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon often takes the place of an implied 'namely,' 'as follows,' 'for instance,' etc.; use a colon when what follows consists of one or more grammatically complete clauses, otherwise use a comma. Put a colon after a salutatory phrase at the start of a letter and after introductory remarks of a speaker addressing an audience. Use a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture and between hours and minutes in time indications. In literary references place a colon between place of publication and publisher. Place the colon outside quotation marks unless it is part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This is true of only two nations ...: Great Britain and France.'; 'My dear Mr. Brown:'; 'Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.'; 'Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan)'. Note exceptions and contrasted constructions given (e.g., use of viz. or 'for instance' may alter punctuation); see discussion and examples in rules 132–136.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons (rules 137–140)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to mark a division of a sentence more independent than that marked by a comma. In enumerations, use semicolons between lengthy or complex linked items, especially when individual clauses contain punctuation. In Scripture references use semicolons to separate passages containing chapters. Place semicolons outside quotation marks unless part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use semicolon in complex lists ('France, 4; Germany, 5; Great Britain, 1 (owing...) ; Italy, 3; the United States, 7.'); between clauses of equal weight ('This is as important for science as it is for practice; indeed...'). See rules 137–140 for extended examples and guidance about interplay with conjunctions such as 'for'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas (rules 141–162)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma indicates the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or construction and contributes to clearness. Rules include separating proper nouns belonging to different individuals/places; serial commas in lists of three or more; when to put commas before/after clauses introduced by common conjunctions; use with introductory adverbs/parenthetical words; use with participial and parenthetical clauses; rules for dates, numbers, places, quoted phrases, and placement inside quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points and examples: always use comma before 'etc.'; serial comma in lists of three or more ('Tom, Dick, and Harry'); omit comma when conjunction connects brief close-knit phrase ('a man good and noble and true'); introductory words like 'however','therefore','moreover' usually followed by comma but exceptions when connection is close; put commas around parenthetical/adverbial/appositional phrases and use dashes for more structurally disconnected insertions (never both together); commas separate identical/closely similar repeated words ('Whatever is, is good'); put comma after thousands (1,276) but not in some journals; separate month and year by comma (November, 1905) except noted journal exceptions; omit comma in certain signature/address lines; comma always placed inside quotation marks. See rules 141–162 for full examples and edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe (rules 163–165)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use apostrophe to mark omission of letters or figures (contractions) and to form possessive case of nouns (add apostrophe or apostrophe + s according to standard possessive rules). Use apostrophe+s for plurals of numerals and rare/artificial coinages; form plurals of proper names ending in sibilants by apostrophe alone for multi-syllable names, and by 's for monosyllabic names ending in s; other detailed forms as given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't; a man's, horses' tails; 'in the 1900's' and 'the Y.M.C.A.'s'; guidance covers contractions, possessives of proper names (Jones's, Themistocles' era), and special pluralization of numerals and coined terms. See rules 163–165.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dashes (rules 166–175)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dash to denote a sudden break, stop, transition, long pause or epigrammatic turn. Use dashes (rather than parentheses) for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent. Use dash to introduce emphatic or explanatory clauses that repeat a word/phrase, to mark 'namely' lists, to precede a final summarizing clause, after side-heads/run-in heads, and before references following a full-sentence quotation in footnotes. Avoid using dash in combination with other terminal punctuation except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Do we — can we — send out educated boys and girls...?'; 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press ... — were the weapons...'; use dash between ranges where appropriate (em/en dash distinctions discussed in rule 173); do not use constructions like 'Dear Sir: — I have...'; see rules 166–175 for examples and notes on when parentheses are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses (rules 176–177)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parentheses to enclose figures or letters marking divisions in enumerations run into text; use standard hierarchicalnotation for outlines and syllabi (A., I., 1., a), (i), etc.). Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses (prefer commas or dashes) unless necessary to avoid confusion or if the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The reasons were three: (1) advanced age, (2) failing health, (3) a desire to travel.' In paragraphed lists, prefer different markers and punctuation styles (capital vs lowercase, italics, periods). See rules 176–177.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets (rules 178–179)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use brackets to enclose an explanation or editor's note, indicate an interpolation or rectification inside a quotation, supply an omission, and for parentheses within parentheses. Use brackets for notices like '[Continued from p. 320]' or '[To be concluded]' centered and italicized in serials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '[This was written before the publication of Spencer's book. — Editor.]'; 'These [the free-silver Democrats] asserted ...'; guidance includes using brackets for editorial insertions and continuations in serialized material. See rules 178–179.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses (rules 180–181)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate the omission of words not essential to the conveyed idea. For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence use four periods (separated by an en-quad) ordinarily; if the preceding line ends in a point do not include that point in the four. For omission of whole paragraph(s) or line(s) in poetry, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads as appropriate; limit the periods to the length of the longest type-line. Treat an ellipsis as part of the citation and enclose it in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and illustrations show four periods for mid-sentence omissions, full-line ellipses for omitted paragraphs, and the need to include ellipses inside quote marks. See rules 180–181 for examples and spacing notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens: general principles (rules 182–214)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphens mark line-break divisions and many compound words. General rules cover hyphenation of compound adjectives before a noun, objective noun compounds (one noun derived from a transitive verb + object), participle+noun compounds (boarding-house), and many family of compounds (book-, house-, mill-, room-, shop-, work- compounds). Guidance enumerates many specific compound classes and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights: hyphenate compound adjectives preceding a noun ('well-known author'); compound nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation often hyphenated ('mind-reader') with listed exceptions ('taxpayer'); present participle+noun compounds and absolute prepositional uses hyphenated ('boarding-house'); compounds with 'book','house','mill','room','shop','work' follow syllable-count rules (one syllable → closed word; two → hyphenated; three or more → two words), with examples; occupation compounds (harness-maker) usually hyphenated; specific rules for prefixes: co-, pre-, re- (use hyphen when same vowel repeats: co-operation, re-enter), quasi- requires hyphen, non- usually hyphenated except common words (nonessential), over-/under- generally closed (overemphasize) with rare exceptions, Latin prepositions ante-/inter-/post- usually closed but exceptions exist (ante-bellum), extra/infra/supra/ultra usually hyphenated, compounds with self- hyphenated, 'half-' and fractional constructions require hyphens, 'like' suffix rules (childlike vs woman-like), 'vice-, ex-, elect' as title-parts hyphenated. Also includes lists of everyday hyphenated words (after-years, cross-section, title-page, etc.). See rules 182–214 for a long list of classes, examples, exceptions, and typographic notes (use en-dash in capitals or when component contains multiple words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word divisions (rules 215–230)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for dividing words at line-ends: avoid unnecessary divisions; in wide measures avoid dividing on a two-letter syllable; never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen; avoid dividing the next-to-last or last line of a paragraph; do not divide proper nouns or separate initials/abbreviations; avoid leaving divisional marks (a) or (i) at the end of a line separated from the text they introduce; prefer American pronunciation-based syllabification over derivation but allow etymological divisions when compatible with spacing and pronunciation; avoid dividing after soft c/g or splitting diphthongs; special rules for derivatives where accent shifts; adjectives in -ical divide on the 'i' (physi-cal); 'do not divide nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and rules: avoid dividing 'only' into on-ly in wide measures; avoid breaking 'process' as proc-ess, prefer pro-cess; divide on vowels where practicable; carry suffix vowel for -able/-ible into next line (read-able); do not create awkward or misleading splits. See rules 215–230 for many concrete examples and typographic constraints (breakline minimum letters, recto/back-of-page guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes / reference indices (rule 231)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices, as a rule, use superior figures (superscript numerals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 231 begins guidance on footnote formatting—use superscript reference figures for indices/footnotes; see following sections (beyond this chunk) for further details on placement and punctuation of footnotes.
